idiom_name: std::chrono::steady_clock fixed-step accumulator paced with std::this_thread::sleep_until
implementation_notes: C++ supplies measurement and a blocking wait but no driver: std::chrono::steady_clock 'represents a monotonic clock. The time points of this clock cannot decrease as physical time moves forward and the time between ticks of this clock is constant', which is why it is 'most suitable for measuring intervals'; std::this_thread::sleep_until 'blocks the execution of the current thread until specified sleep_time has been reached' yet 'may block until after sleep_time has been reached due to process scheduling or resource contention delays'. What replaces the classic structure: nothing hides the loop - the driver is a for(;;) over those two primitives. Use steady_clock rather than system_clock, and rather than high_resolution_clock, which may alias system_clock; keep the accumulator in the clock's own duration type and derive the interpolation alpha from a duration<double> ratio so no integer/float rounding sneaks in. When the application already uses a windowing or engine library (SDL3 callbacks, SFML, raylib, Godot), let that library own the loop instead.
pitfalls: system_clock is wall time and high_resolution_clock may alias it; only steady_clock guarantees a non-decreasing, constant-tick clock, so it is the one to measure intervals with.
sleep_until may overrun because of scheduling or contention; never advance the simulation by the requested duration - recompute elapsed time from steady_clock::now() every iteration.
Sleeping for a whole step wastes the rest of the frame budget when a blocking event wait or vsync could sleep until the next frame, while a loop with no wait at all spins a core.
Floating-point dt accumulates error over long sessions; keep the accumulator in a duration type or double and the step as an exact duration.

variants.name: SDL3 main-callbacks loop (platform-owned)
variants.implementation_notes: The same platform-owned realization C uses is available from C++: define SDL_MAIN_USE_CALLBACKS and SDL calls SDL_AppIterate, which is 'called over and over, possibly at the refresh rate of the display or some other metric that the platform dictates', with events delivered through SDL_AppEvent. What replaces the classic structure: SDL's entry-point machinery and loop replace the hand-written for(;;), which is the documented answer for iOS and Emscripten targets and a way to follow Wayland's frame notifications. Keep the C++ update/render functions as they are and let the callback body call them; the accumulator may still be needed if the simulation must run at a fixed dt independent of the platform's callback cadence.
pitfalls: The C++ object lifetime now spans callbacks: build the app state in SDL_AppInit and free it in SDL_AppQuit, or the appstate pointer dangles.
Do not poll events (SDL_PollEvent/SDL_PumpEvents) inside SDL_AppIterate; SDL delivers them through SDL_AppEvent and manages pumping itself.
The platform decides callback cadence (and may slow it in the background), so any fixed-step simulation still needs measured elapsed time.
